清 玉龍鳳紋韘形珮及玉螭龍紋珮一組兩件

The she (韘) was originally a tool worn on the right thumb by archers to hook and draw the bowstring. From the late Eastern Zhou dynasty onward, it gradually evolved into a type of ornament with a heart-shaped body and openwork designs, known as a she-shaped pendant (韘形珮). Since the late Ming dynasty, the social fashion for collecting antiquities had given rise to a trend of producing archaistic imitations as seen in the present lot. 

See a related jade she-shaped pendant, late Ming/early Qing dynasty, in the Qing Court collection, the Palace Museum, Taipei (acc.no.故玉003260N000000000).

The Wengzhong figure was a type of jade object that emerged during the Han dynasty. According to legend, Ruan Wengzhong 阮翁仲, a formidable and brave general who served under Qin Shi Huang, was stationed at the frontier of the Qin Empire. When Xiongnu invaded, they would flee upon seeing Wengzhong. During the Han dynasty, this legendary figure was consequently fashioned in small jade sculptures, which were worn as protective amulets to ward off evil. A number of Han dynasty jade Wengzhong pendants are in the collection of the Palace Museum, Beijing, illustrated in Compendium of Collections in the Palace Museum: Jade (故宮博物院藏品大系玉器編), vol.4, Beijing, 2011, pls.171-182. 

Later copies were also produced in subsequent periods. See a jade Wengzhong figure, Qing dynasty, and a jade Wengzhong figure, Republic period, both in the Collection of the Palace Museum, Taipei (acc.no.故玉001909N000000000 and 贈玉000252N000000000).

The sinan pendant was a common type of jade amulet worn for apotropaic purposes during the Han dynasty. The spoon on the top represents the directional function of a compass, while also conveying the idea of divination and guiding the wearer towards good fortune and away from misfortune. It was believed that such a pendant should be worn when setting out on long journeys, as a talisman for good fortune. See a similar pendant in the shape of a sinan compass, Eastern Han dynasty, excavated from tomb no.1 at Fenghuangtai, Bozhou, Anhui Province, illustrated in The Complete Collection of Jades Unearthed in China (中國出土玉器全集), vol.6, Beijing, 2005, p.115.

description_block:
Property from the Evaristo Caretti (1879-1955) Collection of Chinese Art 
Lots 25-43

Evaristo Caretti (1879-1955), an Italian, lived in China during the twilight days of the Qing dynasty and throughout most of the Republic period. He first arrived in China as a sailor in the Italian Navy during the Boxer Rebellion. He returned shortly to Italy in 1903, to then quickly return to Shanghai in 1904, where he joined the Chinese Post Office. Mastering Chinese, English and French he was posted to Suzhou, Tangku (Tanggu), Chingwantao (Qinhuangdao), Xi'an, and then in 1912 to Chungking (Chongqing), Changsha in 1914-15, Kweiyang (Guiyang) in 1915-17, Foochow (Fuzhou) in 1918-19, and was granted his first home leave to return to Italy in 1920, where he met his wife in Milan and got married, departing soon thereafter back to China.

On his return he was promoted to a Commissioner rank and posted to Beijing. Between 1925-28 he was Postal Commissioner for the province of Shantung (Shandong), having to deal with both the Kuomintang (Guomindang) party and the Japanese forces. After a third home-leave around 1929 he was transferred to Shanghai as Director of the International Postal Department, and in 1934 he was adviser to China's postal delegation to Egypt. Negotiating the postal agreement with the French Indochina government he was awarded Emperor Bao Dai's Order of the Dragon of Annam, as well as being appointed by Italy's King Victor Emmanuel III as Knight Commander in the Order of The Crown of Italy. Around 1937 Caretti was appointed Director of the Hopeh Postal District, centred in Tientsin (Tianjin). During The Second World War, further to Italy's signing the Armistice with the Allies in September 1943, Caretti and his wife were arrested by the Japanese and sent to a concentration camp near Weihsien (Weixian) in Shantung (Shandong) Province. In 1945 US forces liberated the camp. From there they returned to Tientsin (Tianjin) handing over the postal service to the new staff, and continued to Shanghai where Caretti was pensioned. In 1946-47 Caretti assisted the Italian Navy mission to repatriate all Italians from the Far East, and then returned to Piedmont, Italy, living in Turin.

During this adventurous and tumultuous life, Caretti and his wife Giuseppina, enjoyed collecting and living with Chinese art, from the legendary 1,500-snuff bottle collection, known as 'The Ko Collection' (as he was known in China), to Imperial zitan furniture and porcelain, as well as works of art.A CORAL-RED GROUND SILK EMBROIDERED LADY'S JACKET

description_block:
A RARE GRISAILLE ENAMEL 'BATTLE OF THE SAINTES' PUNCH BOWL
Qianlong, circa 1785
Painted to one side with a panorama of the naval battle between the British and the French in the Caribbean, off the islands of Les Saintes, in 1782, the reverse with a satirical scene depicting caricature figures of an Englishman and a Frenchman, the inscriptions above part remaining reading 'You be damn'd' and 'Vous etes une bete', the interior with a gilt diaper and green enamelled border, with a floral medallion to the well.
33.2cm (13 1/8in) diam.

清乾隆 約一七八五年 墨彩桑特海峽戰役圖盌

This rare bowl is one of a small group made to celebrate the significant naval battle in the Caribbean between the British and the French that took place 9th-12th April, 1782. The maritime scene is taken from a 1783 engraving by Francis Chisholm and John Paltrow after a painting by Robert Dodd (1748-1815). 

The satirical scene is after an engraving titled 'Politeness', which is known in several versions and is attributed to James Gillray (1756-1815) depicting confrontations between national stereotypes and originally published in 1779.

See other examples of this pattern in Hervouët & Bruneau, La Porcelaine Des Compagnies Des Indes A Decor Occidental, 1986, p.49, no.2.38; The Royal Maritime Museum at Greenwich; and Sargent, 2012, Treasures of Chinese Export Ceramics from the Peabody Essex Museum, nos.175,328-329, with more related works listed.

description_block:
A LARGE FAMILLE ROSE 'FILIAL PIETY' VASE, GU
Yongzheng
Of waisted cylindrical form, raised on a tapering foot painted with a lappet band, the body painted with a continuous scene of Yang Xiang raising her hand to subdue a fearsome tiger to protect her father Yang Feng who recoils to her left, having dropped his reaper close by, the scene is set against a mountainous background, with pine trees, bamboo, flowering prunus and chrysanthemums.
49cm (19 1/4in) high.

清雍正 粉彩扼虎救父圖觚

Provenance: An American private collection
Acquired from R & G McPherson Antiques, London, 4th February 2014 (collector's notes)
Peter and Mary White, UK

Published and Illustrated: M. White, Living at the Whites' House: Ceramics from the Mary and Peter White Collection, vol.4, n.p, 2023, p.319

The vase illustrates one of the stories in the Twenty-four Paragons of Filial Piety (二十四孝) when the young girl Yang Xiang protected her father Yang Feng from a fearsome tiger whilst harvesting millet, thereby saving her father's life. She was later rewarded by the country governor with grain and flags.

The vase would have originally formed part of a five-piece garniture comprising two gu-form vases, and three covered jars, each similarly decorated. A related jar and cover, Yongzheng and 65cm high with cover, is held in the collection of the Staatliche Kunstsammlungen, Dresden, inventory no.PO 6037.

description_block:
A BLUE AND WHITE 'HUNDRED ANTIQUES' SEAL PASTE BOX AND COVER
Chenghua six-character mark, Kangxi
The cover decorated with the 'Hundred Antiques' including ancient bronze vessels, an incense tool vase, and a qin wrapped in brocade cloth, the box exterior with four beribboned auspicious emblems. 
6.4cm (2 1/2in) diam. (2).

清康熙 青花博古圖印泥盒及蓋 
「大明成化年製」楷書款 

The decorative theme of the present lot is bogu (博古), which literally means 'appreciation of antiquities,' a long-established aesthetic tradition devoted to the display and contemplation of antique and scholarly objects. From the Song dynasty onwards, rich collectors created dedicated display shelves to showcase their collections of antiquities and curiosities, commonly referred to as bogu shelves. The bogu motif subsequently became an enduring decorative theme, appearing in a wide range of media, including woodcarving, painting, and ceramics, as seen in the present lot.

See a related small blue and white 'Xixiangji' seal paste box and cover, 18th century, which was sold at Bonhams New York, 18 March 2024, lot 85.

一八九六年 馬少宣 玻璃内畫鼻烟壺

The inscription painted inside the snuff bottle, signed by Ma Shaoxuan, is from the Song dynasty poet and politician Ouyang Xiu's 歐陽修 (1007-1072) work 'Ode to the Sound of Autumn' (秋聲賦), which reads:

錄秋聲賦
童子曰：星月皎潔，明河在天，四無人聲，聲在樹間。
余曰：噫嘻，悲哉！此秋聲也，胡為乎來哉。
丙申。馬少宣

And may be translated as:

'Transcribing the Ode to the Sound of Autumn'：
The boy servant says: The stars and moon shine bright. The Milky Way is high up in the sky. There is no human sound, only that of the forest.
I sigh: How sad it is. It is the sound of autumn. Is autumn already here?
Bing shen year.'

A CHINESE EXPORT 'ROCOCO STYLE' WALL HANGING
18th/19th century
Brightly painted in colour and gilt on silk with central floral columns laden with ripe fruits, issuing from arching acanthus leaf swags and delicate flowering and blossoming stems, alternating with pairs of large pink peony blooms, enclosing smaller violet-hued peonies, all on an ivory silk ground, lined.
289cm x 72.5cm (113 3/4in x 28 1/2in).

十八/十九世紀 外銷洛可可式挂屏

This highly decorative wall hanging, produced for the western export market as part of a series, was likely commissioned for a grand European house. The design shows signs of Indian influence, and that of European ceramic motifs. Sometimes Western merchants provided the same design to both Indian and Chinese craftsmen, who used different techniques to produce the products for export. See a similarly designed Chinese embroidered hanging, 19th century, in the Victoria and Albert Museum, accession no. FE.1-1980.

十七至十九世紀 郯子鹿乳奉親玉把件兩件及劉海戲蟾玉把件一件

The story of Tanzi (郯子) is recorded in the Twenty-Four Filial Exemplars (二十四孝), a collection of stories illustrating filial piety. Tanzi's elderly parents suffered from eye ailments and were advised to drink deer's milk. To obtain it for them, Tanzi disguised himself in deer skin and entered the mountains to approach a herd. When a hunter nearly shot him, Tanzi revealed his identity and explained his actions. Moved by his filial devotion, the hunter helped him.

Zhang Zhiwan (張之萬, 1811-1897), courtesy name Ziqing (子青), art name Luanpo (鑾坡), was a Qing dynasty statesman and painter. He was the cousin of another prominent late Qing reforming politician Zhang Zhidong 張之洞 (1837-1909).

Zhang Zhiwan began climbing the bureaucratic ladder of officialdom after being ranked in the top three of the prestigious jinshi degree holders. His first post was as a compiler in the Hanlin Academy. During the Taiping Rebellion, he worked as an advisor for the Qing Court. Around the year 1863, he defeated the peasants of the Nian rebellion in Nanyang and Runan. He held the post of Viceroy of Water Transport between 1866 and 1870 and in 1871, he served shortly as the Viceroy of Minzhe before being promoted to the position of Minister of War.

In 1882, he was conferred the title of Secretary of the Grand Secretariat. In 1884, he gained access to the Grand Council and worked there for ten years. The Imperial Court bestowed the posthumous name Wenda on him. The title he held before his death was the Grand Secretary of the Eastern Pavilion (東閣大學士).

A painted album of twelve leaves by Zhang Zhiwan, depicting landscapes, dated to 1875, is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York (acc.no.1986.267.55a–l).

Provenance: Dr Joseph McDermott (1945-2022), Cambridge, acquired in Japan in the 1980s

Emeritus Reader in Chinese History and Fellow at St John's College, University of Cambridge, Joseph McDermott's (1945-2022) research focused on Chinese social, economic, and cultural history, mainly during the Song, Yuan, and Ming dynasties. A gifted linguist and a generous scholar, McDermott was known for his enduring commitment to Sino-Western academic exchange. His painting collection was mostly acquired in Japan in the 1980s.

This album of thirteen calligraphic fans brings together top scholar-officials of the late Qing dynasty. One of the most important figures represented is Yinghe (1771–1840), a Manchu bannerman and Associate Grand Secretary whose calligraphy was ranked alongside Prince Cheng and Liu Yong, though his career was nearly ended by exile after an Imperial tomb scandal. Shan Maoqian (1807–1879) rose to Grand Secretary of the Wenyuan Pavilion, serving under four Emperors' reigns, while Feng Yuji (1822–1883), a Lingnan child prodigy who served as governor of Shaanxi before being impeached and dismissed in 1883. Song Jin (1802–1874) is remembered for petitioning against the Fuzhou Shipyard, and Xu Pengshou (1821–1866), son of Grand Secretary Xu Naipu, helped settle ritual protocol after the Xianfeng Emperor's death.

Among the other contributors, Feng Peiyuan (1815–1853) placed third in the 1844 examination and drowned himself rather than surrendering to Taiping forces. Mo Zhaowen (d. 1840s) was a Hainan magistrate so beloved that villagers carried his coffin home in a journey spanning over a year. Xiao Junlan (1822–1873) composed a couplet for the rebuilt Tengwang Pavilion and Zhou Xuejun (1810–1858) contributed to the iconic 'Nine Friends of Painting' scroll at the Songyun Temple in Beijing. Mu Weide (1779–1840) served as prefect of Tingzhou before becoming Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments.

description_block:
Various PropertiesA MAP OF CHINA
1851
Ink and colour on paper, painted in three sections, dated to the fourth year of the Kaei period, the map illustrates provinces and major landmarks in China with relevant historical facts, as well as a cursory overview of Joseon, parts of Japan, Ryukyu Islands and Qamil, signed Shizan shosha no and the seal reads Gyokudo next to a table listing Chinese dynasties and corresponding capital cities, enclosed within cover pages and wood box titled Chuka itto zu. 
Approximately 181cm (71 1/4in) high x 264cm (104in) wide overall

一八五一年 《中華一統圖》

The present map was painted at a turning point in history when China's preeminent position in the world was questioned after the early 1840s. Japan had always seen China as Chūka (the Middle Kingdom) - the supreme source of civilisation, philosophy, literature and political order. However, by the late 1840s, Japan's view of China had shifted to a mix of pity and anxiety as it upheld its own isolationist policy known as sakoku.

Japan viewed China as a cautionary tale to aggressively modernise itself according to Western standards but it also experienced deep ambivalence during the process. There was a growing fear of Western Imperialism and its influence on Japanese culture and sovereignty; this led to a social movement known as sonno joi (revere the Emperor, expel the barbarian). The anti-foreign sentiment was accompanied by fascination with ancient China as seen in the present map painted with a special focus on classical Chinese history and tales, offering a glimpse of Japanese scholars' affinity for the classical past. This connection was especially felt by traditionalist Confucian scholars who retained their reverence for classical Chinese culture and blamed the nomadic Manchus for China's decline, they coined the term kai hentai (a transformation from civilised to barbarian).

In fact, the map is titled Chuka itto zu (A Unifying Map of China), yet it includes Joseon and parts of Japan, which seems to position China as a cultural anchor during a period of geopolitical uncertainties and fluctuating cultural identity.

There is a related album of Japanese historical atlas of China titled Tōdo chūko enkakuchi zusetsu, dated 1848, in the University of British Columbia Library, accession no.10.14288/1.0216518.

Compare with a smaller Japanese map of China, dated 1837, sold by Sotheby's London, 7th November 2016, lot 215.

MATSUBAYASHI KEIGETSU (1876-1963)
Showa period (1926-1989), 1937
River Landscape; a six-panel folding screen, ink on gold-washed silk; inscribed at the top with a 56-character Chinese poem, dated hinoto-ushi (1937), and signed Keigetsu sanjin with two seals, the first unread, the second Keigetsu, with a further unread seal at bottom right; with wood storage box bearing the nanatsu boshi (seven-luminary) crest of the Kuki family.
Overall: 173cm (68 3/8in) high x 367cm (144 1/2in) wide; image: 168.5cm (66 3/8in) high x 363cm (142 7/8in) wide. (2).

松林桂月 昭和時代 一九三七年 六扇屏風

Born in Hagi (Yamaguchi Prefecture), Matsubayashi Keigetsu moved to Tokyo at age 18 and was apprenticed to the celebrated Nanga-style painter Noguchi Yukoku. He first showed his work at the annual exhibition of the Nihon Bijutsu Kyokai (Japan Art Association) in 1897 and was selected for the second Bunten national exhibition in 1908; he would continue to exhibit at the Bunten and its successors throughout most of his long life and was appointed to the Teikoku Bijutsuin (Imperial Art Academy) in 1932. Keigetsu was a staunch advocate of the Chinese-influenced Nanga landscape manner and became a leading member of several Nanga associations, including the Nihon Nangain and the Nihon Nanso Gakai. Although he worked in other styles, his most celebrated works are large-scale Nanga compositions, often as here inscribed with long Chinese poems; the present ambitious, expansive screen from the artist's best period was executed in the outsize format fashionable during the early Showa era and very likely shown at one of the regular exhibitions organized by the Nanga associations, but due to current restrictions on library access it has not been possible to confirm this. A wide-ranging fiftieth-anniversary exhibition of Keigetsu's work was held in 2013 at the Nerima Art Museum, Tokyo: see www.museum.or.jp/report/458

description_block:
KATSUSHIKA HOKUSAI (1760-1849)
Edo period (1615-1868), circa 1832
A woodblock print, oban tate-e entitled Mino no kuni Yoro no taki (Yoro Waterfall in Mino Province), from the series Shokoku taki meguri (A Tour of Waterfalls in Various Provinces), circa 1832, published by Nishimuraya Yohachi (Eijudo), censor's seal Kiwame, signed Saki no Hokusai Iitsu hitsu.
37.6cm x 25.5cm (14 3/4in x 10in).

Published in 1832 by Eijudo, the same publisher of his "Thirty-six Views of Fuji", this series consists of eight oban prints of the most famous waterfalls in Japan. In this masterly set of vertical woodblock-print designs, Hokusai further explores water as a dynamic, cosmic, and spiritual force. In several prints the waterfall dominates the pictorial space, typically contrasting the majesty of nature with the tiny, fragile, human elements that feature in some of the designs.

Making liberal use of synthetic Prussian Blue—first imported to Japan only a few years before—in combination with traditional natural yellows, browns, and greens, he created a set of contrasting images of innovative composition and breathtaking variety.

Not confining himself to views that might have been relatively accessible to his core client base in Edo (present-day Tokyo), Hokusai selected spectacular waterfalls throughout central Honshu (Japan's main island) with a focus on sites of religious pilgrimage.

Prints from this series are in the collections of many museums around the world. For examples of this print, see The British Museum, collection no. 1937,0710,0.199; and the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, object no. JP2931.

A complete series was sold at Bonhams New York, 18th September 2024, lot 504.

description_block:
UTAGAWA HIROSHIGE (1797-1858)
Gojusan-tsugi meisho zu-e (Famous sights of the fifty-three stations) ["Vertical Tokaido"]
A complete set of fifty-five woodblock prints, mounted in an album, each sheet signed Hiroshige hitsu, censor's seal aratame (certified), published by Tsutaya Kichizo (Koeido).
Each sheet approx. 36cm x 25cm (14 1/8in x 9 7/8in)

The 514 km long Tōkaidō Road linked the shōgun's capital of Edo (present day Tokyo) to the imperial capital Kyoto. On the highway there were fifty-three halting places. These halting places, together with the starting point at the Nihonbashi (Japan Bridge) in Edo and the finish at Kyoto, make up the fifty-five subjects commonly found in the series of views of the Tōkaidō. Hiroshige created several series depicting the fifty-three Stations - the first known as 'The Great Tokaido' was published in 1833.

In 1855, in collaboration with the prominent publisher Tsutaya Kichizo, Hiroshige released a distinctive set portraying the fifty-three stations along the Tokaido Road in vertical format. These innovative compositional works make use of the paper's vertical structure by using an overhead view to create depth and perspective as well as using Kinzo-gata Kōzu by enlarging objects in the foreground.

For another complete set, see the British Museum, accession no. 1973,0723,0.32.

description_block:
An English Private Collection of Japanese Prints, Lots 298-315SUZUKI HARUNOBU (1724-1770)
Edo period, circa 1768-69
A woodblock print, chuban tate-e, 'Lover Taking Leave of a Courtesan', signed Harunobu ga with a red collector's seal of Hayashi Tadamasa. 
28cm x 21.3cm (11in x 8 3/8in).

Provenance: Hayashi Tadamasa (1853-1906)
An English Private Collection, acquired in the early 20th century and thence by descent.

Hayashi Tadamasa (1853-1906) was one of the first ambassadors of Japanese culture in France. He played a pivotal role in introducing Japanese arts and culture to intellectuals, critics and artists in Europe, contributing to the rise of Japonisme in the late 19th century in Europe. 

The theme of lovers reluctantly parting at dawn often echoes courtly literature. According to The Pillow Book of Sei Shônagon (Makura no sôshi circa 966-1017): 'A good lover will behave as elegantly at dawn as at any other time ... Even when he is dressed he still lingers, vaguely pretending to be fastening his sash ... Indeed, one's attachment to a man depends largely on the elegance of his leave-taking.' Here a high-ranking courtesan (entitled to a luxurious three-futon mattress) catches at her lover's kimono jacket (haori) as he prepares to knot its inner tie. Sake for the cup of parting is on the cabinet behind them.

The man's jacket has a white geometric symbol repeated on the sleeve, which is one of the crests (Genji mon) identifying the chapters in the classic novel The Tale of Genji (Genji monogatari) by Murasaki Shikibu (c.973-1020). References to the novel were often made in this way on prints, although there does not seem to be a specific reference intended here.

Other examples of this print can be found in The Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, accession no. 11.30148 and The Fitzwilliam Museum, Cambridge, accession no. P.3522-R.

A woodblock print, oban yoko-e entitled Echizen Fukui no hashi (Fukui Bridge in Echizen Province) from the series Shokoku meisho kiran (Remarkable Views of Bridges in Various Provinces), published by Nishimuraya Yohachi, signed Saki no Hokusai Iitsu hitsu.
25.7cm x 38.2cm (10 1/8in x 15in).

Provenance: An English Private Collection, acquired in the early 20th century and thence by descent.

Tsukumo bridge, constructed in 1575, is famous for having a wooden northern half, closer to Fukui castle, and a stone southern half. The idea was that the wooden part could be destroyed to prevent an enemy's advance, while the surviving stone part would then make repair easier. Hokusai was clearly fascinated by the bridge, and prominently contrasts the two materials in the foreground. The far bank shows sheets of the renowned local Echizen hōshō paper put out to dry.

An English Private Collection of Japanese Prints, Lots 298-315KATSUSHIKA HOKUSAI (1760-1849)
Edo period, circa 1832
A woodblock print, oban yoko-e, entitled Kumemura chikuri (Bamboo grove of Kumemura village), from the series Ryukyu hakkei (Eight views of the Ryukyu Islands).
25.8cm x 37.5cm (10 1/8in x 14 3/4in).

Provenance: An English Private Collection, acquired in the early 20th century and thence by descent.

Examples of this print can be found in the Art Institute Chicago, Ref. No. 1925.3383. and in the Metropolitan Museum of Art, Object Number: JP2914. The curator notes that Hokusai's prints of the Ryūkyū were probably made to commemorate the Ryūkyū mission's arrival at Edo in November 1832. Although the original gazetteer that inspired Hokusai was in black and white, his series is in exquisite colour. We can see not only his use of colour to heighten the exotic ambiance of the Ryūkyū Islands, but also his imaginative power to make alien islands familiar in the guise of Eight Views.

The curator notes that this view of Mount Fuji is across Sagami Bay, between the trunks of cherry trees that dotted the hills at Goten-yama above Shinagawa, the first post-station on the Tokaido Highway leading south out of Edo.

Kasasagi no
wataseru hashi ni
oku shimo no
shiroki o mireba
yo zo fukinikeri

How the night deepens.
A ribbon of the whitest frost
Is stretched across
The bridge of magpie wings
The lovers will cross.

description_block:
Various PropertiesA NABESHIMA DISH
Edo period, late 17th/early 18th century
The shallow rounded sides rising from a tall cylindrical foot, painted in underglaze blue, red, turquoise and yellow enamels with flowering stems of Eupatorium, the exterior with underglaze blue beribboned brocade roundels above a comb pattern foot.
15.2cm (6in) wide.

江戶時代 十七世紀晚期/十八世紀早期 鍋島燒盤

Eupatorium or Fujibakama are known as one of the seven flowers of Autumn in Japan. The origin of this custom reaches back to the 8th century, in Japan's oldest poetry anthology, the Manyoshu. The poet Yamanoue no Okura wrote a poem noting that there were seven kinds of flowers blooming in the autumn fields, followed by another poem naming these seven flowers, which is said to be the origin of this tradition.

See an example in the Asian Art Museum, San Francisco from the Avery Brundage Collection, object no. B64P15; and another example in the Tokyo National Museum, collection no. G-4762. See an example sold at Christie's London, 11th November 2015, lot 43.

Provenance: Mr Pak-Fei Liu (1914-1984), Hong Kong, thence by descent

Pak-fei Liu (1914-1984) was the oldest son of Budson Liu (1886-1950) whose family legacy stood at the forefront of Hong Kong's luxury goods and services industry for nearly a century. This legacy began in 1920 when family patriarch Budson Liu opened his luxury watch boutique in Central, Hong Kong. The dynasty entered a new era when Pak-Fei Liu expanded into international manufacturing by establishing a watch factory in Japan and distributing Seiko watches throughout Hong Kong and Southeast Asia.

The scene on the cover is possibly from a poem composed by the 8th century Nara period poet Yamabe no Akahito (active 724-736) when he accompanied the Emperor Shōmu to visit Waka-no-ura in Wakayama prefecture today, the poem reads: 'the tide comes in at Waka-no-ura, the lagoon disappears, and the cranes cry out as they fly toward the reed beds'.

「蓬丘堂逸民作」款

Provenance: Lt. Col. Henry Courtney Brocklehurst (1888-1942)
His brother Lt. Col, Sir Philip Lee Brocklehurst Bt, (1887-1975), Swythamley Park, near Macclesfield until 1975
Thence by descent

Exhibited: On long term loan to West Park Museum, Macclesfield, circa 1939-1976

Both brothers were extensive travellers and explorers, Sir Philip having been on Shackleton's 1907 – 1909 Nimrod expedition to the Antarctic and who later travelled through both the Middle and Far East. His brother Courtney, who went with him to the Arctic in 1912 and later became game warden of the Sudan in the 1920s, then went on to travel extensively in China, Japan and Tibet in the 1930s, bringing back the first giant panda from Tibet to the UK.

Many of the artefacts collected on these travels were put on loan at the West Park Museum, which had been built by the Brocklehurst family for safe keeping during the war, and when he was killed in 1942 fighting with the Chindits in Burma, his brother Philip inherited the contents of the museum where they remained until after his death in 1975.

十八/十九世紀 痕都斯坦式葉形壺

Provenance: Sir George Mowlem Burt KBE (1884–1964), Surrey, and thence by descent

Born in Westminster on 10th January 1884, Sir George Mowlem Burt KBE joined the family firm, John Mowlem & Co., in 1902, following in the footsteps of his father and uncle. He subsequently became supervising director of the company and was involved in a number of major engineering and building projects. He was a prominent figure in the development of the civil engineering industry, serving as a founding member of the Federation of Civil Engineering Contractors and on various Government committees and missions. He was also Master of the Worshipful Company of Paviors. Outside his professional life, Burt was a distinguished fencer, winning the British épée championship in 1922 and representing Great Britain in épée at the 1920 Olympic Games. He was knighted in 1942 and died at Blindley Heath, Surrey, on 1st September 1964. An enthusiastic collector of art, his collection included paintings, ivory, netsuke and jade.

description_block:
A MOTHER-OF-PEARL-INLAID BLACK LACQUER TRAY
Wan Wangning three-character mark, Ming Dynasty
Of square form with canted corners, the centre finely decorated with a terraced pavilion scene depicting two gentlemen and a lady, all dressed in luxuriant long robes, accompanied by a deer and attendants, another lady gazing down from a pavilion, and a toad at the lower left exhaling misty clouds enclosing two dancing ladies and the Moon Hare preparing the Elixir of Longevity, the well decorated with four panels, each enclosing a pair of Mandarin ducks, the exterior sides encircled by foliate flower-heads. 37.6cm (14 3/4in) square.

明 黑漆嵌螺鈿蟾宮人物圖盤
「萬王寧」楷書款

Provenance: An English private collection 

The present lot is a fine example of the craftsmanship and design of Ming dynasty mother-of-pearl-inlaid lacquerware. The openwork cutting of the shell inlays on the luxuriant garments of the three principal figures is refined and may represent a technical hallmark of the mid-Ming dynasty. A comparable design and technique can be observed in the depiction of two female figures on a mother-of-pearl-inlaid black lacquer dish, 16th century, in the collection of the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York. For further discussion and illustration, see East Asian Lacquer: The Florence and Herbert Irving Collection, New York, 1991, pp.135-136.

The present lot employs the 'thin mother-of-pearl inlay' technique (薄螺鈿 bo luodian), a refined method originating in the Song dynasty. This technique is distinguished by the use of delicate shell inlays, merely 0.1–0.3mm thick, in contrast to the 'thick mother-of-pearl inlay', which typically ranges from 0.5–2mm. Also frequently referred to as 'soft mother-of-pearl inlay' (軟螺鈿 ruan luodian), this technique involves soaking the shell material in vinegar to increase its pliability, allowing it to conform seamlessly to both flat and curved surfaces as seen in the present lot. For further discussion on this technique, see Fu Juyou, 'Bo luodian qiqi' (薄螺鈿漆器), in The Forbidden City (紫禁城), 2008(11), pp.136-147. 

The female figure at the centre holding a fan may represent the Queen Mother of the West, while the male figure beside her, dressed in a dragon robe, could depict King Mu of Zhou (?-c.922 BCE). The Tale of King Mu, Son of Heaven (穆天子傳 Mu tianzi zhuan), a Warring States Period text (475-221 BC), recounts King Mu's journey to the Queen Mother of the West. At the Jade Pool, the Queen Mother received King Mu with lavish hospitality. Additional motifs, such as the toad and the hare, are associated with the Moon Palace, further enriching the scene's cosmological and auspicious symbolism. 

See a related mother-of-pearl-inlaid black lacquer octagonal oblong tray with similar mist-clouds and figural imagery, 15th/16th century, which was sold at Bonhams New York, 15th March 2021, lot 130.

拉斐爾·佩特魯奇 《遠東藝術中的自然哲學》

Provenance: Laurence Binyon's copy, with dedication from the author (the Petrucci volume)

A connoisseur's study of the painting of China and Japan, and the copy presented to the author's closest friend and colleague Laurence Binyon (see Hatcher, John Laurence Binyon, Oxford, 1995, p.169). Both were fascinated by Chinese art, and among the earliest scholars attempting to interpret it for the western public.

Raphael Petrucci, Marquis of Siena (1872-1917), studied Chinese art and language under Edouard Chavannes in the first decade of the twentieth century, and rapidly became an authority on Chinese painting and Buddhist iconography. He was 'one of the ablest and most devoted students and interpreters of the art of the Far East'. An Italian based in Brussels, his house was filled with his collection of Chinese and Japanese art. Petrucci worked on the collection of Chinese and Tibetan paintings brought back from Tun-huang by Sir Aurel Stein for the last three years of his life.

Laurence Binyon, in his introduction to Petrucci's later book, Chinese Painters: A critical study, wrote of Raphael Petrucci, 'His most important work ... is La Philosophie de la Nature dans l'Art d'Extrême-Orient, a sumptuously printed folio published by Laurens in Paris, with illustrations by the Kokka Company, and written with as much charm as insight. Petrucci's knowledge of Chinese gave him an authority in interpreting Chinese art which writers on the subject have rarely combined with so much understanding of art in general, though as a connoisseur he was sometimes over-sanguine. His translation from a classic of Chinese art-criticism, originally published in a learned magazine, has lately appeared in book form.'
